guide.title: SoMa, San Francisco: the Yerba Buena museums, the Old Mint and the warehouse blocks
guide.intro: SoMa is short for South of Market, and Market Street is its northern edge. It is a district of warehouses, printing lofts and narrow service alleys into which the late twentieth century inserted a museum quarter, and both halves are still legible from the pavement. The Yerba Buena blocks around Third and Mission Streets hold the San Francisco Museum of Modern Art, the Museum of the African Diaspora, the Yerba Buena Center for the Arts and Moscone Center, with Yerba Buena Gardens between them. On Fifth Street stands the Old San Francisco Mint, San Francisco Landmark No. 236, designated in 2003. Elsewhere run Minna, Natoma, Clementina and Tehama, the service alleys of the old grid, and the brick warehouse blocks around South Park that the city protects under Article 10 of the Planning Code.

sections.heading: The Yerba Buena blocks
sections.body:
The museums here are addressed on three streets, and it is worth having the numbers before you arrive. The San Francisco Museum of Modern Art is at 151 Third Street. The Museum of the African Diaspora is at 685 Mission Street, on the ground floor of the St. Regis. The Yerba Buena Center for the Arts has its galleries at 701 Mission Street and its theatre at 700 Howard Street. The Contemporary Jewish Museum is at 736 Mission Street, the Children's Creativity Museum at 221 Fourth Street and Moscone Center at 747 Howard Street. Saint Patrick's Church, San Francisco Landmark No. 4, designated in 1968, stands at 756 Mission Street; the city's Article 10 record gives its address as 748 Mission Street.

Two of them will not let you in at present. The Contemporary Jewish Museum is temporarily closed and no source states a reopening date, so no hours are given here. The Museum of the African Diaspora is closed for exhibition installation from 17 August to 29 September 2026 and reopens on 30 September 2026.

Yerba Buena Gardens, at 750 Howard Street, is the open ground the museums face. Its own site gives daily opening from 6am to 10pm, with public restrooms open 9am to 5pm. The Martin Luther King Jr. Memorial stands inside the gardens, and the Yerba Buena Ice Skating Center and the Yerba Buena Bowling Center sit on the Moscone roof deck within them. No source states opening hours for the rink or the bowling centre, so none are given here.

sections.heading: Getting there
sections.body:
No source establishes a transit stop, a bus route or a station entrance for these addresses, and no distances or travel times are given here. Steer by street numbers instead.

Market Street is the district's northern edge, and a street has two sides. The Market Street addresses in this quarter are on its south side: the Palace Hotel at 633–665 Market Street, the Hobart Building at 582–592 Market Street, the Mutual Savings Bank Building at 700 Market Street, the building at 735 Market Street and Hale Brothers Department Store at 901 Market Street. Yerba Buena Lane and Mint Plaza are pedestrian cuts through the block between Market Street and Mission Street, and Mint Plaza faces the Old Mint at 88 Fifth Street.

The lamp standards along Market Street itself are the Path of Gold Light Standards, San Francisco Landmark No. 200, designated in 1991, and the city's Article 10 record gives their address as 1–2490 Market Street. They run the whole length of the street rather than standing in any one district.

The museums cluster on Third, Fourth, Mission and Howard Streets. The older fabric is spread much wider: Tenth Street for the James Lick Baths at 165 Tenth Street, Howard Street for St. Joseph's at 1401 Howard Street, Otis Street for the Juvenile Court and Detention Center at 150 Otis Street, Twelfth Street for the San Francisco Eagle Bar at 398 Twelfth Street, Brannan Street for SOMArts at 934 Brannan Street, Clementina Street for the American Bookbinders Museum at 355 Clementina Street, and First, Bryant and Townsend Streets for the warehouse blocks.

sections.heading: Landmarks and districts
sections.body:
Article 10 of the Planning Code is the city's own protective register, and SoMa carries a run of its numbers. The Old San Francisco Mint at 88 Fifth Street is San Francisco Landmark No. 236, designated in 2003, and was listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 1966, reference number 66000231. St. Joseph's Catholic Church at 1401 Howard Street is San Francisco Landmark No. 120, designated in 1980, and was listed on the National Register of Historic Places, reference number 82002250. The James R. Browning United States Court of Appeals Building at 95 Seventh Street was listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 1971, reference number 71000188, and designated a National Historic Landmark.

Others carry an Article 10 number alone: the James Lick Baths, the New Pullman Hotel on Townsend Street, the Hotel Utah building on Fourth Street, Mint Mall and Hall on Mission Street, the Oriental Warehouse on First Street, the Piledrivers, Bridge and Structural Ironworkers Local No. 77 Union Hall on Bryant Street, the Palace Hotel on Market Street and the San Francisco Eagle Bar on Twelfth Street.

The same register also covers whole blocks rather than single buildings. The South End Historic District was designated under Article 10 of the Planning Code, Appendix I, on 23 March 1990 by Ordinance 104-90. The Clyde and Crooks Historic District was designated under Article 10 of the Planning Code, Appendix O, on 3 December 2018. Several other district names circulate for this part of the city — the SoMa LGBTQ district, the South Park district, the Sixth Street lodging houses, the Western SoMa light industrial blocks — and the city's own historic-district file records each of them as eligible rather than as a designation under Article 10 of the Planning Code. Eligible is not the same thing, and no protection attaches to a building because it stands inside one of them.

faq.question: What does SFMOMA cost, and when is it open?
faq.answer: The San Francisco Museum of Modern Art is at 151 Third Street, 94103. Its own site gives Monday and Tuesday 10am to 5pm, Wednesday closed, Thursday noon to 8pm, and Friday to Sunday 10am to 5pm. Admission is $30 for adults, $25 for seniors 65 and over, $23 for students, and free for anyone 18 and under.

faq.question: Which SoMa museums cannot be visited at the moment?
faq.answer: The Contemporary Jewish Museum at 736 Mission Street is temporarily closed and no source states a reopening date. The Museum of the African Diaspora at 685 Mission Street is closed for exhibition installation from 17 August to 29 September 2026 and reopens on 30 September 2026; on reopening its hours are Tuesday, Wednesday, Friday, Saturday and Sunday 11am to 5pm, Thursday noon to 8pm, closed Monday. The San Francisco Museum of Modern Art, the Yerba Buena Center for the Arts, the Children's Creativity Museum and the American Bookbinders Museum are open, each with hours on its own site.

faq.question: Can you go inside the Old Mint?
faq.answer: Not as a museum. The Old San Francisco Mint at 88 Fifth Street is used for special events, some of them open to the public, and no source states opening hours, so none are given here. The building is San Francisco Landmark No. 236, designated in 2003, and was listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 1966, reference number 66000231. Alfred B. Mullett designed it and it was built between 1 April 1869 and November 1874, in Greek Revival style.

faq.question: Is South Park a protected historic district?
faq.answer: No. South Park is a public open space set between Second, Third, Bryant and Brannan Streets, and the South Park Historic District named for it is recorded by the city as eligible on the California and National Registers, which is not a designation. The Article 10 district in this quarter is the South End Historic District, designated under Article 10 of the Planning Code, Appendix I, on 23 March 1990 by Ordinance 104-90, with a period of significance running from 1867 to 1935.

faq.question: What is free to see in SoMa?
faq.answer: Yerba Buena Gardens at 750 Howard Street opens daily from 6am to 10pm at no charge, and the Martin Luther King Jr. Memorial stands inside it. The Yerba Buena Center for the Arts is free to members, to anyone 17 and under and to military personnel, and free to all on Wednesdays; otherwise it is $10 for adults and $5 for students and seniors. The Museum of the African Diaspora is free to all on the second Saturday of each month and free to children under 12. The warehouse fronts and alley grid of the South End Historic District cost nothing to walk.

faq.question: Is anything in SoMa on the federal register?
faq.answer: The Old San Francisco Mint at 88 Fifth Street was listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 1966, reference number 66000231, and designated a National Historic Landmark in 1961; it is also California Historical Landmark No. 875. The James R. Browning United States Court of Appeals Building at 95 Seventh Street was listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 1971, reference number 71000188, and designated a National Historic Landmark. James Knox Taylor, Supervising Architect of the Treasury, designed the courthouse and it was built between 1897 and 1905.

places.name: San Francisco Museum of Modern Art
places.summary: The city's modern and contemporary art museum, on Third Street. Its own site gives Monday and Tuesday 10am to 5pm, Wednesday closed, Thursday noon to 8pm, and Friday to Sunday 10am to 5pm. Admission is $30 for adults, $25 for seniors 65 and over, $23 for students, and free for anyone 18 and under.
places.history: No source states an institutional history for the museum, so none is given here.

places.name: Yerba Buena Gardens
places.summary: The open ground the Yerba Buena museums face, entered from Howard Street. The gardens' own site gives daily opening from 6am to 10pm, with public restrooms open 9am to 5pm. The Martin Luther King Jr. Memorial, a wall of falling water with inscribed texts, stands within the gardens.
places.history: The Yerba Buena Ice Skating Center and the Yerba Buena Bowling Center sit on the Moscone roof deck inside the gardens. No source states opening hours for either, so none are given here.

places.name: Museum of the African Diaspora
places.summary: A museum on the ground floor of the St. Regis, at Mission and Third Streets. It is closed for exhibition installation from 17 August to 29 September 2026 and reopens on 30 September 2026. Its hours are Tuesday and Wednesday 11am to 5pm, Thursday noon to 8pm, Friday to Sunday 11am to 5pm, closed Monday. Admission is $15 for adults and $7 for seniors, students and educators; children under 12 enter free, and entry is free to all on the second Saturday of each month.
places.history: No source states a founding date for the museum, so none is given here.

places.name: Yerba Buena Center for the Arts
places.summary: A contemporary arts centre with galleries at 701 Mission Street and a theatre at 700 Howard Street. Its own site gives Wednesday 11am to 8pm, Thursday to Sunday 11am to 5pm, closed Monday and Tuesday. Entry is free to members, to anyone 17 and under and to military personnel, and free to all on Wednesdays; otherwise it is $10 for adults 18 and over and $5 for students and seniors.
places.history: Fumihiko Maki designed the galleries and forum. James Polshek, with Todd Schliemann, designed the theatre.

places.name: Contemporary Jewish Museum
places.summary: The Contemporary Jewish Museum is temporarily closed and no source states a reopening date, so no hours are given here. The building at 736 Mission Street is Daniel Libeskind's 2008 addition wrapped around the Jessie Street Substation, which Willis Polk designed in 1907. The substation is San Francisco Landmark No. 87, designated in 1977, and was listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 1974, reference number 74000555.
places.history: Willis Polk built the substation in 1907; Daniel Libeskind's addition of 2008 is wrapped around it, so the two are one building.

places.name: Children's Creativity Museum
places.summary: A hands-on museum for children inside Yerba Buena Gardens, entered from Fourth Street. Its own site gives Wednesday to Sunday 10am to 4pm.
places.history: The LeRoy King Carousel in the gardens is run by the same organisation.

places.name: Moscone Center
places.summary: The city's convention centre, on Howard Street. It is a working exhibition and meeting building rather than a visitor attraction in its own right, and access depends on whichever event is in the halls.
places.history: Its roof deck carries the Yerba Buena Ice Skating Center and the Yerba Buena Bowling Center, which stand inside Yerba Buena Gardens.

places.name: American Bookbinders Museum
places.summary: A working collection of bookbinding machinery on Clementina Street, one of SoMa's alleys. Its own site gives Tuesday to Saturday 10am to 4pm. Admission is $15 general, $12 for seniors 62 and over and for young people aged 10 to 17, and free for children under 10. There is a self-guided audio tour and the building is wheelchair accessible.
places.history: No source states a founding date for the museum, so none is given here.

places.name: SOMArts Cultural Center
places.summary: A city-owned arts centre of 26,000 square feet on Brannan Street. Its own site gives Thursday 3pm to 7pm, Friday noon to 7pm, Saturday and Sunday noon to 5pm, closed Monday to Wednesday.
places.history: The centre grew out of the Neighborhood Arts Program, which the San Francisco Arts Commission created in 1967. SOMArts became an independent 501(c)(3) organisation in August 1979.

places.name: Old San Francisco Mint
places.summary: The Old San Francisco Mint stands at 88 Fifth Street, facing Mint Plaza. It is not open as a museum. The building is used for special events, some of them open to the public, and no source states opening hours, so none are given here.
places.history: The Old San Francisco Mint stands at 88 Fifth Street. Alfred B. Mullett designed it and it was built between 1 April 1869 and November 1874, in Greek Revival style. It is San Francisco Landmark No. 236, designated in 2003, and was listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 1966, reference number 66000231. It was designated a National Historic Landmark in 1961 and is California Historical Landmark No. 875. In 2003 the federal government sold the building to the City of San Francisco for one dollar — an 1879 silver dollar struck at the mint.

places.name: James R. Browning United States Court of Appeals Building
places.summary: The James R. Browning United States Court of Appeals Building stands at 95 Seventh Street, on the northeast corner of Seventh and Mission Streets. James Knox Taylor, Supervising Architect of the Treasury, designed it, and it was built between 1897 and 1905. It was listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 1971, reference number 71000188, and designated a National Historic Landmark. It houses the United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit.
places.history: No source states visiting arrangements for the building, so none are given here.

places.name: Saint Patrick's Church
places.summary: A Gothic Revival Catholic church of 1872 on Mission Street. It is San Francisco Landmark No. 4, designated in 1968. The city's Article 10 record gives the address as 748 Mission Street.
places.history: No source states opening hours or mass times for the church, so none are given here.

places.name: St. Joseph's Catholic Church
places.summary: A Gothic Revival church of 1913 on the corner of Howard and Tenth Streets, designed by John J. Foley. It is San Francisco Landmark No. 120, designated in 1980, and was listed on the National Register of Historic Places, reference number 82002250. The city's Article 10 record gives the property as 1401 Howard Street and 240 Tenth Street.
places.history: The building is deconsecrated. No source states current public access, so none is described here.

places.name: Jackson Brewery Co. Complex
places.summary: The Jackson Brewery Co. Complex stands at 1475–1489 Folsom Street and 319–351 Eleventh Street. It is San Francisco Landmark No. 199, designated in 1991, and was listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 1993, reference number 93000284.
places.history: The city's Article 10 record gives the building date as 1912, names James T. Ludlow and Kaufman & Edwards as its architects, and describes the style as Romanesque Revival.

places.name: James Lick Baths
places.summary: A Richardsonian Romanesque bathhouse of 1906 on Tenth Street. The city carries it under two names, James Lick Baths and People's Laundry. It is San Francisco Landmark No. 246, designated in 2004.
places.history: The city's Article 10 record names Wright & Sanders as the architects and gives the building date as 1906.

places.name: New Pullman Hotel
places.summary: A Classical Revival building of 1909 at 228–248 Townsend Street. It is San Francisco Landmark No. 280, designated in 2018.
places.history: The city's Article 10 record gives the building date as 1909 and the style as Classical Revival, and names no architect.

places.name: Hotel Utah
places.summary: A Classical Revival and Edwardian corner building of 1908 at 500–504 Fourth Street. It is San Francisco Landmark No. 282, designated in 2018. Businesses trade under variants of the Hotel Utah name at this corner; no source establishes which occupies which address, so no operator is named.
places.history: The city's Article 10 record gives the building date as 1908 and the style as Classical Revival and Edwardian, and names no architect.

places.name: Mint Mall and Hall
places.summary: A building at 951–957 Mission Street. It is San Francisco Landmark No. 321, designated in 2025.
places.history: The city's Article 10 record gives no architect, style or building date for the property.

places.name: Juvenile Court and Detention Center
places.summary: An American Renaissance civic building of 1914 on Otis Street, designed by Louis Mullgardt. It is San Francisco Landmark No. 248, designated in 2006, and was listed on the National Register of Historic Places, reference number 11000182.
places.history: No source states public access to the building, so none is described here.

places.name: San Francisco Eagle Bar
places.summary: A leather bar on Twelfth Street, in the run of clubs and bars along the Mission edge of the district. Its own site gives Monday 6pm to midnight, Tuesday closed, Wednesday and Thursday 6pm to midnight, Friday and Saturday 2pm to 2am, and Sunday 1pm to midnight.
places.history: The building dates from 1906. It is San Francisco Landmark No. 295, designated in 2021, and the city's Article 10 record gives the property as 396–398 Twelfth Street.

places.name: DNA Lounge
places.summary: A music venue and nightclub on Eleventh Street. No source states its opening hours, so none are given here; its programme sets when it opens.
places.history: No source states a history of the venue, so none is given here.

places.name: Palace Hotel
places.summary: A hotel of 1909 filling the block front at 633–665 Market Street, on the south side of the street. It is San Francisco Landmark No. 18, designated in 1969, and the city's Article 10 record names the designated property as Palace Hotel, Garden Courtyard.
places.history: The city's Article 10 record gives the building date as 1909 and names Trowbridge & Livingston and George Kelham. No source states its rates, so none are given here.

places.name: Hobart Building
places.summary: An office building at 582–592 Market Street, on the south side of Market. It is San Francisco Landmark No. 162, designated in 1983, and was listed on the National Register of Historic Places, reference number 100006911.
places.history: It is a working office building and no source states public access, so none is described here.

places.name: Mutual Savings Bank Building
places.summary: A bank building at 700 Market Street, on the south side of the street. It was listed on the National Register of Historic Places, reference number 13001107.
places.history: No source states public access to the building, so none is described here.

places.name: Building at 735 Market Street
places.summary: A commercial building on the south side of Market Street, carried on the federal register under its street number rather than a name. It was listed on the National Register of Historic Places, reference number 04000327.
places.history: No source states an architect, a building date or public access for it, so none is given here.

places.name: Hale Brothers Department Store
places.summary: A department store building at 901 Market Street, on the south side of the street. It was listed on the National Register of Historic Places, reference number 86003492, and a boundary increase covering 36 Fifth Street and 423–427 and 429 Stevenson Street was listed under reference number 01000490.
places.history: No source states public access to the building, so none is described here.

places.name: Oriental Warehouse
places.summary: A brick vernacular warehouse of 1867, addressed both as 620–650 First Street and as 650 Delancey Street. It is San Francisco Landmark No. 101, designated in 1977.
places.history: The city's Article 10 record gives the building date as 1867 and the style as brick vernacular warehouse, and names no architect. No source states public access, so none is described here.

places.name: Piledrivers, Bridge and Structural Ironworkers Local No. 77 Union Hall
places.summary: A Classical Revival union hall of 1909 on Bryant Street. It is San Francisco Landmark No. 281, designated in 2018.
places.history: The city's Article 10 record gives the building date as 1909 and the style as Classical Revival, and names no architect.

places.name: Gran Oriente Filipino Hotel
places.address: 95 Jack London Alley, San Francisco, CA
places.summary: A Filipino masonic temple and hotel building on Jack London Alley. The Gran Oriente Filipino Hotel is recorded on the National Register of Historic Places under reference number 100004869.
places.history: A separate city file for the Gran Oriente Filipino Complex carries no Article 10 number, so no city designation attaches to the wider group of buildings.

places.name: South Park
places.address: South Park Street, San Francisco, CA
places.summary: An oval green set inside a block bounded by Second, Third, Bryant and Brannan Streets, with houses and small businesses facing it on all sides. It is open ground and no admission is charged.
places.history: The South Park Historic District named for it is recorded by the city as eligible on the California and National Registers, which is not a designation.

places.name: South End Historic District
places.summary: The South End Historic District was designated under Article 10 of the Planning Code, Appendix I, on 23 March 1990 by Ordinance 104-90. Its period of significance runs from 1867 to 1935. It covers warehouse and industrial blocks in the streets around Second Street, Townsend Street and South Park.
places.history: It is a set of protected street blocks rather than a site with an entrance, and there is nothing to book or pay for. The city's file also records a South End Historic District Addition, which is eligible only and carries no protection.

places.name: Clyde and Crooks Historic District
places.summary: The Clyde and Crooks Historic District was designated under Article 10 of the Planning Code, Appendix O, on 3 December 2018. The city gives its period of significance as 1906 to 1935.
places.history: It is a set of street blocks rather than a site with an entrance, and there is nothing to book or pay for.

places.name: Second and Howard Streets District
places.summary: A small commercial district at Second and Howard Streets, taking in 121–198 Second Street, 579–612 Howard Street, 116 Natoma Street and 111–163 New Montgomery Street. It was listed on the National Register of Historic Places, reference number 99000894.
places.history: The city gives its period of significance as 1906 to 1912.

places.name: Haas Candy Factory
places.summary: A former candy factory at 54 Mint Street. It was listed on the National Register of Historic Places, reference number 00001622.
places.history: No source states an architect, a building date or public access for it, so none is given here.

places.name: National Carbon Company Building
places.summary: An industrial building at 599 Eighth Street. It was listed on the National Register of Historic Places, reference number 83001233.
places.history: No source states an architect, a building date or public access for it, so none is given here.

places.name: Building at 465 Tenth Street
places.summary: A building on Tenth Street, carried on the federal register under its street number rather than a name. It was listed on the National Register of Historic Places, reference number 99000581.
places.history: No source states an architect, a building date or public access for it, so none is given here.

places.name: Victoria Manalo Draves Park
places.summary: A city park on Folsom Street, with a community garden and Bessie Carmichael School adjoining it. It is named for Victoria Manalo Draves, a Filipina-American diver born in SoMa.
places.history: No source states an opening date for the park, so none is given here.

entries.name: San Francisco Museum of Modern Art
entries.note: Open 10am to 5pm most days, closed Wednesdays and noon to 8pm on Thursdays; $30 for adults and free for anyone 18 and under.

entries.name: Yerba Buena Gardens
entries.note: Open ground at 750 Howard Street from 6am to 10pm daily, holding the Martin Luther King Jr. Memorial and, on the Moscone roof deck, the ice rink and bowling centre.

entries.name: Museum of the African Diaspora
entries.note: Closed for exhibition installation until 29 September 2026 and reopening on 30 September; $15 for adults, and free to all on the second Saturday of each month.

entries.name: Yerba Buena Center for the Arts
entries.note: Galleries by Fumihiko Maki at 701 Mission Street and a theatre by James Polshek with Todd Schliemann at 700 Howard Street; free to all on Wednesdays.

entries.name: Old San Francisco Mint
entries.note: Alfred B. Mullett's Greek Revival mint of 1869 to 1874, San Francisco Landmark No. 236, designated in 2003; it is not open as a museum and no source states hours.

entries.name: Contemporary Jewish Museum
entries.note: Temporarily closed with no stated reopening date; the building is Daniel Libeskind's 2008 volume wrapped around Willis Polk's Jessie Street Substation of 1907.

entries.name: Children's Creativity Museum
entries.note: Hands-on studios for children inside Yerba Buena Gardens, open Wednesday to Sunday 10am to 4pm, with the LeRoy King Carousel beside it.

entries.name: American Bookbinders Museum
entries.note: Working bookbinding machinery on Clementina Street, open Tuesday to Saturday 10am to 4pm, $15 general, with a self-guided audio tour.

entries.name: James R. Browning United States Court of Appeals Building
entries.note: James Knox Taylor's courthouse of 1897 to 1905 at Seventh and Mission Streets, listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 1971, reference number 71000188.

entries.name: Saint Patrick's Church
entries.note: A Gothic Revival church of 1872 facing Yerba Buena Gardens across Mission Street; San Francisco Landmark No. 4, designated in 1968.

entries.name: South Park
entries.note: An oval green inside the block bounded by Second, Third, Bryant and Brannan Streets, with houses and small businesses facing it on all sides.

entries.name: South End Historic District
entries.note: Warehouse and industrial blocks designated under Article 10 of the Planning Code, Appendix I, on 23 March 1990, with a period of significance from 1867 to 1935.

entries.name: SOMArts Cultural Center
entries.note: A city-owned gallery and performance space of 26,000 square feet on Brannan Street, out of the Neighborhood Arts Program the Arts Commission created in 1967.

entries.name: San Francisco Eagle Bar
entries.note: A leather bar in a building of 1906 at 398 Twelfth Street; San Francisco Landmark No. 295, designated in 2021.

links.note: SoMa's neighbour across Eleventh and Twelfth Streets, with Mission Dolores, Dolores Park and the Valencia Street corridor.
West along Market Street: the War Memorial Opera House, Davies Symphony Hall, Alamo Square and the Market Street Masonry Historic District.
The ballpark and the China Basin waterfront, at the bay end of Third Street.
The other side of Market Street and then some: Grant Avenue, the Dragon Gate and the Chinatown alleys.
